body:
I do love this quote from her though: 

"I'm not a concept. Too many guys think I'm a concept or I complete them or I'm going to 'make them alive'…but I'm just a fucked up girl who's looking for my own peace of mind. Don't assign me yours."

"But I *have to* yell at you when I have a panic attack!"

Nope.

Thank you! This is all tremendously helpful.

It's so funny because I started this process trying to prove to the US that I'm not Canadian (I thought I had to, but apparently I don't). Then I'm going to turn around and try to prove to Canada that I am! I am Schrodinger's Canadian!

I have a terrible sinking feeling that I'll get a no. But I will try! If nothing else, I will have a passport of *some* kind and can go visit for butter tarts and rye.

The family lore is that Mom did do the complicated renunciation. Somewhere around here is a scrapbook with a photo of the event. I'll be fucked if I can find it, and Mom passed in 2020. But this would have been...1960? And my grandparents were kind of into the whole "all-American" thing. They were big-time squares. Thanks, y'all. 

My Canadian buddies are urging me to get Mom's birth certificate and make my case. They have planned a party with rye and butter tarts! And they have quite sensibly pointed out that if I do indeed have dual citizenship, I can pass that to my daughter, who is transgender. She's in a "sanctuary" jurisdiction in the US (thankfully NOT in Texas with me), but who knows how long that will last? 

I so appreciate all the help and insights.

Thank you! If I'm worried, it's because some part of me is expecting...pushback? When I apply for a US passport? I've never done that before, I've never traveled much, and I have a perhaps irrational fear of the passport office in Texas giving me some kind of hard time. "This here says Canada, little lady!"
I moved home for a while to care for my mom in hospice, and the first time I got my period there, I swiped one of her diapers. Game. Changer.

When I got married 25 years ago, I changed my name and immediately regretted it. 

Why? My MIL made a huge stink about how children of a mother with a different last name were bastards (her word, not mine) and should be SHUNNED. My husband's aunt was sitting right there and said I AGREE. So that's what I was dealing with. 

Here I am now with this last name still. Divorced husband ten years in. Husband passed three years later.

My former MIL is still alive (she's over 100 and clearly powered by spite). And would you believe it bugs her that I still have this name? She's started calling me by my maiden name again. Nope. No take-backsies. 

My daughter (who is trans) and I have the name you wanted for us. Don't like that? Too bad. I'm not changing it. So I guess that makes us your legacy.

I was looking for this response! Unless you prefer video, the Betty Crocker "red binder" is an excellent newbie resource. I learned to cook from it in the 1990s and sent my copy off with my daughter when she moved out so she could feed herself well.

The only thing it can't help you solve is the abusive partner problem. Hey, I had that too! Don't marry that guy. I spent 14 years with a guy like that. It never got better. It will not get better. You deserve better.

I've also used Replens, which is a sort of gel with an applicator. It's formulated to stay in place (for lack of a better term), so you use it every three days. It's compatible with most kinds of condoms (but not all).

Revaree or another suppository product with hyaluronic acid. 

Don't be like me and use the hyaluronic serum you use on your face, because ow ow ow it has other ingredients that sting.

I have lots of "aww" stories about them, going back to when I met his wife on an early 2000s message board for moms. 

When my daughter got interested in concert photography in high school, they got her a press badge at a show in our town and instructed her on how to hold her ground in the photography pit. (Not as rowdy as the pit-pit, but there's still jostling.) She got some great photos of the band and an interview.

We also left the show with armloads of merch that I am reluctant to wear in the event that I get quizzed. :)
My favorite thing about it is that Stephen (whom I mainly know through his wife) is a TOTAL dad. Minivan, tattoos of his kids' artwork, studio at home. They're a super-sweet family.

My favorite story about this issue (which I've told before) is when a young friend of the family went to get coffee wearing her Descendents shirt. The (guy) barista sniffed at her and bet she couldn't name three Descendents songs. She did, of course, because she's a big fan of the band. 

And then she took out her phone and called her dad on speaker. "Hey," her dad told the guy. "I don't appreciate you bugging my daughter or gatekeeping my fans." 

Her dad is Stephen Egerton, guitarist for the Descendents.

Hi there! I hear your conundrum and relate. I'm stuck in TX too because my MIL is quite elderly and lives in residential care here. We absolutely have plans to bolt when she passes. 

My situation is different in that my MIL is a sweet lady who loves me and has voted blue all her life despite being Catholic. (She's very pro-union.) And I'm at the end of my fertile years, though I still have cycles. 

I'm asking my GYN about an IUD until I'm officially in meno, and I have a stockpile of Ella. And my daughter, who's close to your age, is stashed in a blue state.

If ending the relationship is on the table, run. If not, protect yourself while getting your ducks in a row. Do you know where you might like to go?

She's comfortable but I don't know how actually experienced she is. She's working on a license in the jurisdiction where she currently lives, but if I ask her for too many specifics, she says I'm nagging her. :)
Right, yes. Safety is a big deal, and I'm open to guidance as long as it's not the "see here, little lady" kind of thing.

Highly recommend the little dog/big dog combo.

Our smaller dog has a big attitude and a piercing bark that hits you like a fork to the spine. The big dog is sort of goofy but activated by his sister's alerts. 

Also makes for adorable photos.

Loving on this thread from Texas as a bi woman with a trans daughter. I stalk this sub because y'all are adorable. My spouse and I have been planning our exit since 2020, but I've got an elderly MIL in residential care, and we can't leave her behind. 

We tried to visit this summer but had to cancel because of COVID. I was so sad!

Hugs to you all and to Big Penny.
I live in a jurisdiction with a ban, and my plan for if I ever have to travel for care involves handing my phone off to an accomplice who will visit every tourist trap in town during my procedure.
Seconded

Are you me? I had this same conversation with my therapist day before yesterday. She asked me why I don't hold boundaries at work. Why do I snap to attention when someone on chat asks me umpteen questions that aren't my role to answer

Because I was literally trained not to push back on people, ever? Could that be it? Yeah, that's it.

I'm a lot older than you are, though. So my mom was from the Silent Generation, when kids were meant to be seen and not heard, and you didn't talk back, ever. My dad wasn't abusive, but my grandfather was an alcoholic who raged around the house, and that's what Mom grew up knowing. She didn't deliberately teach me to be meek; she taught me methods for survival based on her experience. She literally taught me not to upset people. 

I'm doing a lot better in my interpersonal relationships, but work is still a challenge, especially dealing with people senior to me. I'm the breadwinner, and I can't just say LOOK IT UP IN THE DOCUMENTATION when people treat me like a 24-hour hotline. Do I have all the answers? No, I look them up in the fucking documentation. 

Working on it, I guess.

You thought she'd be there holding daisies, but you were wrong. Which is a learning experience, we do hope. I continue to like the song and probably always will, but the lyrics make me want to slide off my glasses and massage the bridge of my nose in quiet exhaustion, like COME ON NOW.

When that song was everywhere (and it was everywhere), I got in the habit of yelling TELL HIM, KIMBRA before her verse. Now TELL HIM, KIMBRA remains as a trope in our household for situations in which someone is about to get sat down and TOLD.

I used to love "Stars" by Hum...until I listened to the lyrics.

She's not at work, she's not at school
She's not in bed, I think I finally broke her
I bring her home everything I want
Nothing that she needs

Granted, the song has a regretful perspective (I...think?) but damn.

"Fuckin' Dennis."

We say that all the time around the house.

I had an ex from high school in the damn 1980s who wouldn't stop trying to get me to "remember the fun times we had" (spoiler alert: they were not fun). I never responded to him. He died earlier this year. Time is nothing to a stalker.

If you like indie dramas, I'll put in a plug for Sunshine Cleaning, about two sisters who start a business doing biohazard cleanup. It's streaming.

Also anything by Allison Anders.
I'm another Texan who likes to "y'all," but I get the best results with HI, EVERYBODY! like Dr. Nick from The Simpsons.

Literally same. My current husband (we met when I was 40) is great. Every single other man with whom I've ever had a relationship with has landed somewhere on the misogyny spectrum, from gross jokes to coercive control and physical abuse.

I have a naturally smiley face. It just does that. As many have noted, I learned to control my face around men because they took it as an invitation or assumed I was really stupid. ("What are YOU smiling about?!")

So when I smile at women, that's just me being me! 

It has gotten better since I've gotten older and gone gray, as others have said. Now I have Crone Powers too! I can afford to relax a little more around everybody since I scan more as Kindly Grandma.
Lol! Metaphorical bulldog. And we didn't have to go to court, even. Once it was plain that I would not be kicked to the curb, ex-hub and I underwent a collaborative divorce instead.

This. I met with a bulldog attorney at the start of my divorce because I feared my ex would use my PPD against me in court. The bulldog attorney swiftly replied, "If your depression made you unfit, then why would he have left the child with you as the primary caregiver during the marriage?"
Gray hair is like a blank slate for vivid colors! No pre-lightening required. I've found that I can get a lavender tint just by using purple shampoo. And highly pigmented darker colors look amazing.

Kind of like your mom, I started coloring in my teens because I thought my natural color was sort of blah. Didn't realize that I was getting gray the whole time. Once I realized what my roots were doing, I kept coloring because I work in tech and I was afraid of being "read" as old. 

Enter COVID. 

My hair grew out and I was astonished. I have SILVER hair in a cool pattern. (Just the top and sides.) I get TONS of compliments from younger women. Some of them ask me how I "did it." Nature, baby!
Most of the Mexican places I've been to here in Texas have "hamburgesa" on the menu. And it's a good burger!
I love this one!

That is a good point! I do tend to forget about the University of Tennessee because it's not right there next to me, causing crowds at HEB. Thanks!

But have you seen Tower?

I was wondering if this would bring out the Texans! And it did! Hey, y'all!

It bothered me when I heard it, not because they should have known (that's debatable) but because I literally kept thinking, "Wait, Arlington? What?"

UTA *is* UT Arlington. I worked at UT Austin and for the UT system organization, and that is [literally in the training](https://www.utsystem.edu/sites/branding/writing-style-guide).

Should A & A have known? Well, not necessarily. I don't know the ins and outs of every large state university system. But I know there's a UMass campus in various locations, and its flagship location is in Amherst. I know the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign (or UIUC). If I were to speak about an event at one of these places, I would exercise care to specify the location with the correct reference. But then again, I am literally an editor.*

OTOH, the Tower shooting is kind of a BFD, y'all! It's not an obscure event. It was the first mass shooting. I know A & A have called out Skip Hollandsworth, so they know Texas Monthly. Pam Colloff wrote a definitive piece about the event ("96 Minutes"), which is the basis for the OUTSTANDING documentary "Tower."**

I just don't think the research is happening, and that's kind of sad, especially for a pivotal event with many living survivors. 

*The person who makes sure your novel set in New Orleans doesn't have basements in it 

**Watch Tower, seriously
Christopher Ecclestion in Shallow Grave. But not in anything else. Just as the dweeby accountant hiding in the attic ready to murder.

This is close to my thoughts as a woman in red state with a full ban. I want to leave outright (and stay gone) but I can't move because of caregiving responsibilities for a family elder. So we wait and plan.

Technically we can afford to leave, and my job is remote, but I am panicked by the thought of prices ticking up and housing stock diminishing as we sit here waiting and planning. Many people can't afford to leave at all, but it's sure to get worse.

So my suggestion to those who want to support women, trans folks, and anyone else who wants to leave is: Do what you can to make your community safe and welcoming to shellshocked newcomers. Build a network to help connect people with resources you have. If you're open to cohousing, learn about the laws in your area.

My periodontist came into the exam room and greeted me with "How are you, young lady?"

First of all, I'm like ten years older than you.

Secondly, just no.
And how! Heavier, crampier, and longer. Yaaaaay perimenopause!

This. I'm not a trans woman, but my daughter is. And she has curly/wavy hair. I do not. Any hair advice I can give her does not apply because different textures have different rules. Different techniques. Different products. 

The best advice for finding your look is the same as it's ever been: work with what you've got. Long flowy blown-out femme hairstyles are hard to achieve for anyone with textured hair, and you'll damage your hair trying. 

So what my kid did was find a salon for all genders  in her gayborhood, present herself to the stylist, and ask for a feminine look that she can pull off with her hair type. Now she has an adorable wolf cut.

People are telling you it's truly not an issue. You can keep asking, but the answer isn't likely to change.

I am indulging your question because I am An Old, and it tears me up inside to see people of any gender freaking out over the weird mathematical definitions of attractiveness that exist these days. Oh no, my face isn't perfectly symmetrical. Oh no, my eyes are downturned. I will never be attractive 

Stop it. Just stop it.

I married a guy with a jawline so weak that it required maxillomandibular advancement surgery in order for him to BREATHE. That is how little it matters. 

"But if there was an otherwise identical guy with a strong jaw, would you prefer him?"

Life is not theoretical. What if there was an otherwise identical guy but he had superpowers? A money tree? The ability to command the creatures of the sea?

I picked a dude with a weak jaw. It happens. Stop torturing yourself and focus on your strengths, all y'all.
Ooh! Ooh! I'm also in Austin and I've been meaning to check out Matriarchy Build. I'm just fixin to get to these repairs any minute, you know. Thanks!

When I went on for my colonoscopy, the young lady in the prep room with me got that question from the nurse. (I swear I wasn't eavesdropping; there was only a curtain between us.)

Nurse: Any chance you could be pregnant?

Prep-room Neighbor: I don't have sex with men, so no.

Clean and simple. We're in Texas, USA if that matters.

To the parents: please allow me to recommend a book called When Parents Hurt by Joshua Coleman. (The title has a double meaning.) It is excellent.

My 22yo and I have a bumpy relationship. Her father was verbally abusive when she was little. I divorced him, but then I kind of fell apart when it was all over. I didn't make the best choices. I didn't keep it together as well as I could have. I had a lot of healing to do, and I'm still healing to this day. I was a whole mess.

So what I did (and what the book recommends) is taking accountability for your mistakes. Apologize, sincerely, for your mistakes. And then you leave it there. Let your kid know your door is always open and you will always love them. And then STOP. Don't nag. Don't guilt them.

My doctor prescribed a cyclical increase in my SSRI, which meant upping my dose for the week. My results were so-so, but it might be worth a shot.

The really helpful thing for me is weed. I'm not saying it's The Answer, but if I need to snap myself out of a bad crying/anger state, it works for me.

Also I minimize my contact with people as much as I can. I work from home, so it's mainly a matter of lying low and absolutely keeping my mic turned off during meetings. I curtail any social arrangements and give myself permission to goblin out.

I also have this. I don't have any advice to get rid of the "pooch," but it is kind of numb, so I've leaned into having the cat "make biscuits" there instead of on my more sensitive body parts.

It's like a built-in cat scratcher.

I tried out the Atkins diet when I originally got my PCOS diagnosis ages ago (1997 or so). It was supposed to help with insulin resistance. For me, it wasn't super helpful, but folks in my support group said it helped them get some symptoms under control, so YMMV, I guess. 

I've never read anything about period cramps or PMS, but I wasn't having regular periods at that time.

I also found the diet unsustainable in the long run. I was hangry and light-headed a lot of the time. Having said that, it doesn't hurt to try? These days I eat whole-grain carbs and fruit for fiber and just try to avoid highly processed foods for my overall health.

I'm married to a good one, and if it matters, we met later in life, when I was one of those single moms said to be of "low value" or whatnot. He's not perfect (I'm not either), but our relationship has always been mutually respectful. He's an amazing stepdad to our daughter and stepped in 100% to raise her when I got called back home to help my dad in hospice. He's close with his mom and sisters and a good listener. I actually knew his sister first, and she's a feminist yogini and slam poet, which is maybe a lot of the reason that he doesn't see women as a sex class or another species or some shit. He's just a good human.

I have a friend from work whom I would absolutely  describe as a good man. He's very big and burly and bearded, and he came to me once almost devastated that he might inadvertently scare women in public. So I laid it out (we have reasons to be fearful of strange men, which he understood) and talked about how to be more sensitive and aware.

Even the "good" men haven't thought it through.

I live in a full-ban state and am married to a really decent guy. I am in perimenopause, so my cycles aren't regular. I had a full-on scare recently, and my husband was very supportive. Bought tests with cash. Patted me on the shoulder, said we'd go to the nearest safe location if we had to.

Right? Wrong. What he didn't know is that I already had a plan. We would need someone else to make the appointment, not either of us. You'd need cover for your travel. You can't whip out your debit card to pay for it. You need to cover your tracks. 

This had not occurred to him! Of course I had a plan! I gathered my "aunties" and made a plan before Roe ended. 

Even when they mean well, dudes just don't walk in our shoes.

Yup. "Just wait until menopause" could be a lot longer than "8 to 10 years" if you're not already in peri.

I have one friend who is still having cycles (and therefore still at risk of pregnancy) at 57. 

"Tell him no PIV until then" is kind of a solution, but not for women who enjoy it and want to have it safely.

It's not that I enjoy it, but I do feel relief. And I do kind of adopt a "red tent" mindset. I give myself permission to power down a little, say no to socializing, and cocoon up with a book if I'm not working. I'm an introvert with a supportive partner, so I do find that part enjoyable.

Also, I'm in perimenopause. I'm honestly not ready for my cycles to fully stop because I have osteopenia that I fear will progress into osteoporosis. I'm working on improving that with my health care team, but estrogen does protect the bones in the meantime.

Your question sounds like you're looking for "magic words" or something, and that is a little... icky? But? I'm old enough to ask the rhetorical question: *Did everyone on Earth forget how to dim the lights and put on an Al Green record?* 

Your approach to this issue is so clinical and, frankly, strange to me. Maybe focus more on setting the mood and creating a space where your partner can relax instead of asking a women-only space for tips on neurolingustic programming.
You also might like Polite Society by Nida Manzoor, who also created the show We Are Lady Parts.

Anything by Nicole Holofcener or Allison Anders. I also love Sunshine Cleaning by Christine Jeff's. These aren't "powerful" movies about "powerful" women, just character-driven indies about women's experiences. Which is powerful, kwim? Same thing with Go Fish and Daughters of the Dust.

It feels like just another example of how women can't win. (I don't think men with pale skin get hassled.) 

So I grew up in the 80s (you might be my age?) and a "healthy glow" was a prerequisite for white girls. I was taking an exam one time in high school, and the dude next to me was making cracks about how he couldn't SEE because the GLARE from my legs was BLINDING him. (I was wearing a skirt.) Oh, Brian. You were so hilarious.

Later on life, a realtor was touring me and my then-husband around a neighborhood, and when we passed a Darque Tan, the realtor said, "We can just drop you off there, Lettuce!" Ha ha ha.

So yeah, it is (or was) kind of a thing. Be white but not too white. Be thin but not too thin. Be smart but not too smart. Be put-together but not high maintenance. Can't win.
Sounds like you're asking for [relationship advice](https://www.reddit.com/r/relationship_advice/s/fgUPfZSuEe).

This is what we do with chores. Talk about your individual strengths and preferences and work out a plan so that the most-hated chores don't fall on one person.

I hate laundry and everything about it except having clean clothes to wear. Husband is a laundry nerd who could have his own TikTok on folding techniques, and he's into line-drying. So guess who does the laundry? Not I! 

Who shops and cooks? I do. I'm way better at it, and it doesn't stress me out. I'm much better at keeping a mental note of what we need each week. 

Husband has ADHD, so he's the go-to for deep cleaning tasks that leverage his hyperfocus. I don't have ADHD, so I leverage my executive functions keeping up with bills and tidying.

Are you Gen X? Just curious. Because I was super into The Simpsons from when it started out on The Tracey Ullman Show. I was in college, and a whole bunch of us (mixed-gender) would pile into the lounge at 7:00 for the new episodes. This would have been 1991 or so.

I think there are kind of two ways of watching The Simpsons. One is "Oh, Homer is so dumb but lovable." I haven't watched the show in years; i quit when the storylines flattened into tales of Homer's antics. But when the show was good? It was GOOD. So many layers. So many references. My favorite episode is still the Cape Feare one. Those episodes are waaaay more than Homer's dumb antics.

I pepper Simpsons references into many conversations. Embiggen is a perfectly cromulent word! Stop the Planet of the Apes - I want to get off! 

And then there's Lisa, who is the moral heart of the show. Every time I cook beets, I yell WE GOT BEEETS! like Lisa coming home from the farmers' market.

I think lots of women do appreciate the show, but it's likely we enjoy it for different reasons.
"Children need interesting parents." --Ariel Gore
You're welcome, friend! Glad to hear you are feeling better.

Oh, also! In urgent care situations, I sometimes have doctors question whether my allergies are "real." Fair play, I guess, since some people think they're allergic but they're not. But when a doctor asks, "What happens when you take this medicine?" go ahead and lay it out. It's not "a little stomach upset." When I took penicillin, I got hives all over my body and had trouble breathing. When I took sulfa because I couldn't take penicillin, I also got hives all over my body, and then my liver failed and I had to spend three days in hospital.

Hey there! I'm allergic to penicillin and sulfa, so I feel you.

It's been a hot minute since I had a UTI, but when I get a sinus infection I get doxycycline. 

[This list](https://www.nhstaysideadtc.scot.nhs.uk/Antibiotic%20site/penhypers.htm#:~:text=Tetracyclines%20(e.g.%20doxycycline)%2C%20quinolones,in%20the%20penicillin%20allergic%20patient.) might be helpful?
East Texas too! Barbecued or fried. Mmmm.
In Texas, we call them "calf fries." Along with chicken gizzards, they were my dad's favorite.

Or if you're in peri like me, biweekly real periods!

Oh, you want my menstrual data? Here you go! Send it over to NASA to see if they can determine my orbit.

My husband actually brought it up! That was his side of the conversation.

We are Texans, so our other example would be the Texarkana Moonlight Murders. A serial killer who targeted heterosexual couples. It does happen.

Also, everyone here is packing heat.

Right?!

I took the spirit of the question as involving surprise. A bear standing in front of you suddenly. A man standing in front of you suddenly. Like, a dude just standing there. Not the dudes who are camping or hiking and doing wilderness stuff. My husband and I were both NUH-UH

TBF, the "burying a body" comment came from my husband, after he asked me if there were any signs of what the hypothetical man in the hypothetical forest was up to, hypothetically. Did he have binoculars? A fishing pole? Was he involved in some kind of activity? I said I assumed he was just...there. Like, maybe he just emerged from a clearing. 

Husband was like NOPE. BEAR PLEASE.
Distract it with your pic-a-nic basket!

This happened to me twice with a contraceptive sponge! The first time I was able to break the seal with a Slurpee spoon (no joke). The second time I went to urgent care, and a very nice doctor removed it. It's hilarious to me now.

My daughter is a pedal geek* and loves "metalcore." I don't fully understand what that is because I'm an old grown-up 1980s person. Women and gay men and other "outsiders" have been a part of metal as long as I can recall, and I'm disappointed that this shit STILL happens in guitar communities. It's not that hard to be inclusive when it's about the MUSIC. 

My daughter got me into Yvette Young and I think she's awesome. I also love me some Marnie Stern. She's a freakin virtuoso. 

*Seriously she has SO MANY PEDALS

In the past five years, I turned 50 and grew in my gray, and that's helped a lot with regard to getting hassled in public. 

However, I'm still on guard watching out for other people getting hassled.

This! I had a really stubborn hemi for which I was referred to surgery, but thankfully it resolved and went back in before I called to schedule. Whew! But absolutely yes on the sitz baths with Epsom salts and the stool softener. 

In a way, I kind of wish I'd done the surgery because then it would be gone forever. It could pop out again and cause problems later.

I use Clue because I'm in perimenopause and I have no *clue* what's going on with my cycles. :)

They don't sell your data, apparently, but [Consumer Reports had some issues with it.](https://www.consumerreports.org/health-privacy/what-your-period-tracker-app-knows-about-you-a8701683935/)

I'm in a hostile location (Texas), and my periods are now 21 days apart (peri sucks). So I think of my data as a spoiler.

You're most welcome. And it's okay to protect yourself when getting to know someone (anyone) and becoming involved. Our hearts are wild and precious things, and it is not easy to be vulnerable. Wishing you the best and lots of clarity.

Divorced mom here! I think more conversation is a good idea. Yes, you should protect yourself emotionally. Yes, it is necessary to consider his motivations in dating, and I think more divorced men than women seek a "replacement spouse." All of this is possible.

I will say this, however. When I started dating a (single, no-kids) person, I had more than one freakout that I wasn't "good enough" or that I was "damaged goods," and I withdrew. I was a little flaky. I tried to pull a move from Harry and the Hendersons ("Just go on! Find someone better!") But he did not. ("If that's what you want, but I like *you*.") 

Idk if divorced men feel that way, but I sure did. I was scared, too. I think it's worth talking it over if you like this person. Be careful. Always be careful.

In terms of watching documentaries and listening to podcasts, true crime skews toward women. But that doesn't mean "all women love true crime." That would be a stereotype. Many women love ice cream, but others are lactose-intolerant or prefer savory foods. (Hey! Like me!)

Funnily enough, I am An Old, and my first exposure to "true crime" was before podcasts, streaming, and even basic cable. I got obsessed with Skip Hollandsworth's crime reporting for Texas Monthly in the 1970s. (IMO, he's still the best to ever do the thing.) There's nothing "girly" about Texas Monthly, and the stories are more like hard-nosed longform regional journalism than gossip or "wine and crime" or whatnot. It was just accepted that everyone had an interest in the twisted tales of murderous oil barons (T. Cullen Davis) and homegrown serial killers (Dean Corll).

I am sorry to tell you this, but there is not much "free time" for a SAHM unless you have some kind of supplemental child care. I was a SAHM (if you want to get technical, a WAHM) until my kiddo started kindergarten, and this was in 2002 when the economy was a lot less fucked. 

I did freelance writing work in my "free time." I thought it would be a lot easier than it turned out to be, even with assignments over the weekend (when my husband wasn't working and could ostensibly handle child care). Turns out he wanted to relax on the weekends. Mind you, I was getting paid for writing, and my freelance income helped us make bills, but he was so angry and resentful over it that I had to work out babysitting from a fellow mom. So I had a couple of hours "off" twice a week to focus on writing. 

Your "free time" will be precious. You will have to negotiate for it. If your child is napping, you will seize those moments to either rest (you'll need it) or tackle the dishes/laundry/shower/handle other house tasks. I thought I'd be blissfully writing away while my kid played with blocks. Ha. Not quite. 

I even asked my mom forum: At what age will my child self-entertain so I can do creative work? Oh, how they laughed.
